newsitem.title: INDIA: Former Thai premier Chatichai sees economy safe.
newsitem.headline: Former Thai premier Chatichai sees economy safe.

text.p: Thailand's economic fundamentals are sound and foreign investors confident about the economy's inherent strength, former Thai prime minister Chatichai Choonhavan said on Wednesday.

"Our economic fundamentals remain sound, and foreign investors are confident in the Thai economy's resilience," Chatichai, who leads the second largest party in the ruling coalition, told a business meeting in the Indian capital.
Chatichai, who is also chairman of Thai Prime Minister's advisory committee on economic and foreign affairs, said the government will strongly defend the value of embattled baht.
"Strongly we will defend the value of our baht," said Chatichai, who leads the Chart Pattana Party (CPP).
Chatichai was visiting India as a special emissary of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and was accompanied by a 10-member delegation.
Asked if the government would be well advised to expand the basket of currencies linked to the baht, Chatichai said: "Not at this time."

The baht came under speculative attack in May on rumours it may be devalued amid a chronic economic crisis facing Thailand, but stabilised after a successful defence by the Bank of Thailand with the help of regional central banks.

Thailand is suffering its worst economic crisis in more than a decade, hit by high interest rates, a sharply slowing economy, sluggish exports and a liquidity crunch which has affected the finance and property sectors.
Chatichai said the Bank of Thailand estimates that gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 5.9 percent in 1997, down from 6.4 percent last year.

Surakiart Sathirathai, vice chairman of Prime Minister's Advisory Council on Economic and Foreign affairs said: "The right and correct macroeconomic policy direction will shore up confidence of foreign investors both in Thailand and abroad as to how we will cope with current account deficit and how we will go with our budget."

Surakiart Sathirathai, a former Thai finance minister, told Reuters the government had, earlier in the week, initiated measures to deal with shortage of liquidity in the financial markets, crisis in property market and a slump in exports.

He said the measures that have come out and will be coming out next week will assure the public that these were measures that can really help the property market, ease problems of the financial institutions and revive exports.

The government on Tuesday issued four urgent decrees to avert a crisis in the finance and property sectors. The executive decrees sought to allow greater foreign equity participation in new banks and merging finance firms.
Finance firms are saddled with billions of dollars in non-performing loans, mostly to the property sector.

"The government has no policy of devaluating the baht and the government has to defend the baht and will be defending the baht," Surakiart Sathirathai said, when asked if the government will continue to defend the baht.

"But my opinion is that if we can shore up confidence, of how you will deal with sub-sectoral problems, as how you will do with current account deficit in long-run, then there will not be any need to defend the baht," he added.
"Because then people will have confidence in the baht."
